Nonlinear stability of composite waves of traveling wave and rarefaction wave for a parabolic-hyperbolic system arising from chemotaxis 00footnotetext: *Corresponding author. 00footnotetext: E-mail addresses: liust533@nenu.edu.cn (S. Liu), lijy645@nenu.edu.cn (J. Li)

Sitong Liu, Jingyu Li Affiliation: School of Mathematics and Statistics, Jiangxi Normal UniversityNanchang, 330022, P.R.China Affiliation: School of Mathematics and Statistics, Northeast Normal UniversityChangchun 130024, PR China

Abstract: We study the nonlinear stability of a composite wave consisting of a traveling wave and a rarefaction wave for a parabolic-hyperbolic system arising from chemotaxis. We prove that if the initial value is a small H1H^{1}-type perturbation of composite wave, then the system admits a global solution that converges toward the composite wave with an absolutely continuous shift. The proof combines the weighted relative-entropy mechanism for viscous shocks with the energy structure of rarefaction waves. A key ingredient is the inclusion of a rarefaction modulation factor in the weighted relative entropy; its derivatives combine with the terms generated by the rarefaction profile to produce a rarefaction dissipation. Moreover, the spatial separation of the two waves yields time-integrable interaction errors caused by the non-exact superposition. Since diffusion acts only on the density component, the full H1H^{1} estimate is closed by exploiting the coupling structure of the system to recover the missing dissipation of the hyperbolic component.

Key words: Chemotaxis; parabolic-hyperbolic system; composite wave of traveling wave and rarefaction wave; nonlinear stability; relative entropy.

AMS(2020) Subject Classification: 35B35, 35L65, 35Q92, 92C17

1 Introduction

In this paper, we study the large-time behavior of solutions to the Cauchy problem for the one-dimensional parabolic-hyperbolic system

{nt−(n​q)x=nx​x,x∈ℝ,t>0,qt−nx=0,x∈ℝ,t>0,\begin{cases}n_{t}-(nq)_{x}=n_{xx},&x\in\mathbb{R},\ t>0,\\ q_{t}-n_{x}=0,&x\in\mathbb{R},\ t>0,\end{cases} (1.1)

subject to

(n,q)​(x,0)=(n0,q0)​(x)⟶(n±,q±)as ​x→±∞.(n,q)(x,0)=(n_{0},q_{0})(x)\longrightarrow(n_{\pm},q_{\pm})\qquad\mbox{as }x\to\pm\infty. (1.2)

The system (1.1) is derived from the PDE–ODE hybrid chemotaxis model with logarithmic sensitivity

{nt=nx​x−(n​(ln⁡c)x)x,ct=−n​c+β​c,\begin{cases}n_{t}=n_{xx}-\big(n(\ln c)_{x}\big)_{x},\\ c_{t}=-nc+\beta c,\end{cases} (1.3)

which was introduced by Levine et al. [19] in the modeling of the interaction between vascular endothelial cells and the vascular endothelial growth factor during the initiation of tumor angiogenesis. Here n>0n>0 denotes the cell density and c>0c>0 the concentration of chemical signal. The logarithmic sensitivity reflects the Weber–Fechner law and, at the same time, produces a singularity at c=0c=0; see, for example, [1, 6, 17]. The Hopf–Cole transformation introduced by Levine and Sleeman [18],

q:=−(ln⁡c)x=−cxc,q:=-(\ln c)_{x}=-\frac{c_{x}}{c},

removes this singularity and transforms (1.3) into (1.1).

The Cauchy problem for (1.1) has been studied extensively around constant background states. Guo et al. [10] established global strong solutions for large initial data. Zhang et al. [32] constructed global classical solutions near positive constants and derived algebraic decay, while Li et al. [20] developed entropy estimates yielding global well-posedness for large classical solutions. Related multidimensional well-posedness results can be found in [20, 8, 11]. When the end states in (1.2) are different, however, the large-time dynamics are governed by nonconstant wave patterns associated with the Riemann problem for the inviscid system

{nt−(n​q)x=0,qt−nx=0,\begin{cases}n_{t}-(nq)_{x}=0,\\ q_{t}-n_{x}=0,\end{cases} (1.4)

with

(n,q)​(x,0)={(n−,q−),x<0,(n+,q+),x>0.(n,q)(x,0)=\begin{cases}(n_{-},q_{-}),&x<0,\\ (n_{+},q_{+}),&x>0.\end{cases} (1.5)

Writing (1.4) as

(nq)t+(−q−n−10)​(nq)x=0,\binom{n}{q}_{t}+\begin{pmatrix}-q&-n\\ -1&0\end{pmatrix}\binom{n}{q}_{x}=0, (1.6)

we obtain the characteristic speeds

λ1​(n,q)=−q−q2+4​n2<−q+q2+4​n2=λ2​(n,q),\lambda_{1}(n,q)=\frac{-q-\sqrt{q^{2}+4n}}{2}<\frac{-q+\sqrt{q^{2}+4n}}{2}=\lambda_{2}(n,q), (1.7)

and the corresponding right eigenvectors

rk(n,q)=(−λk(n,q),1)T,k=1,2.r_{k}(n,q)=(-\lambda_{k}(n,q),1)^{T},\qquad k=1,2.

Moreover,

∇λ1​(n,q)⋅r1​(n,q)\displaystyle\nabla\lambda_{1}(n,q)\cdot r_{1}(n,q) =−1−qq2+4​n≠0,\displaystyle=-1-\frac{q}{\sqrt{q^{2}+4n}}\neq 0, (1.8)
∇λ2​(n,q)⋅r2​(n,q)\displaystyle\nabla\lambda_{2}(n,q)\cdot r_{2}(n,q) =−1+qq2+4​n≠0, if n>0.\displaystyle=-1+\frac{q}{\sqrt{q^{2}+4n}}\neq 0,\text{ if }n>0.

Thus, in the region n>0n>0, the inviscid system is strictly hyperbolic and both characteristic fields are genuinely nonlinear.

The Riemann structure of (1.4) contains shocks, rarefaction waves and their superpositions. Wang and Hillen [31] constructed shock waves for the inviscid system and the corresponding traveling waves of (1.1). The one-dimensional stability theory for such traveling waves under zero-mass perturbation was subsequently developed in [23, 13, 22]; Li, Wang and Zhang [21] also treated a composite wave of two traveling waves. An important advance was made by Choi, Kang, Kwon and Vasseur [3], who introduced a weighted relative entropy and a time-dependent shift and proved an aa-contraction property for a small traveling wave, allowing arbitrarily large perturbations at the level of the relative entropy. This contraction estimate was then used by Choi, Kang and Vasseur [5] to obtain global well-posedness for large H1H^{1} perturbations of a small traveling wave.

Two more recent developments are especially relevant to the present work. First, Liu, Li and Xu [26] established nonlinear stability of planar traveling waves for the three-dimensional version of (1.1) under general perturbations. Their argument combines the relative-entropy method with a time-dependent shift in the basic estimate and exploits intrinsic cancellations of the chemotaxis system in the higher-order estimates, thereby removing the zero-mass restriction that is inherent in the classical anti-derivative framework. Second, Liu and Li [25] established the asymptotic stability of strong rarefaction waves for (1.1), including both a single rarefaction wave and a superposition of two rarefaction waves. In that setting the wave strength is not required to be small. The key ingredients are the monotonicity of the smooth rarefaction approximation in both space and time and the use of the coupling structure of (1.1) to recover the missing dissipation of the hyperbolic component.

These two mechanisms do not simply superpose when a rarefaction wave and a viscous shock are present simultaneously. This is the main issue addressed in the present paper. We consider a 1-rarefaction wave connecting (n−,q−)(n_{-},q_{-}) to an intermediate state (nm,qm)(n_{m},q_{m}) and a 2-viscous shock wave (i.e. traveling wave) connecting (nm,qm)(n_{m},q_{m}) to (n+,q+)(n_{+},q_{+}). We prove that, when the two wave strengths and the initial perturbation are small, the resulting composite wave of traveling wave and rarefaction wave is asymptotically stable under general H1H^{1}-type perturbations.

To formulate the result, define the kk-rarefaction curve through a state (n−,q−)(n_{-},q_{-}) by

Rk(n−,q−)={(n,q)∈ℝ2:hk(n,q)=hk(n−,q−),λk(n,q)≥λk(n−,q−)},R_{k}(n_{-},q_{-})=\left\{(n,q)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}:h_{k}(n,q)=h_{k}(n_{-},q_{-}),\ \lambda_{k}(n,q)\geq\lambda_{k}(n_{-},q_{-})\right\}, (1.9)

Our main theorem is the following.

We next explain the main novelties and the proof strategy. The first difficulty is that the two components of the composite wave have very different dissipative mechanisms. The traveling wave is spatially localized and has a neutral translation mode. Its stability is therefore naturally measured by a weighted relative entropy with a time-dependent shift, as in [3, 26]. In contrast, the smooth rarefaction wave spreads in space and its favorable terms come from monotonicity of the profile, as in [25]. If one applies the shock contraction estimate to the composite profile without modification, the derivatives of the rarefaction profile generate additional terms that are not controlled by the shock dissipation alone.

To overcome this obstruction, we introduce, in addition to the shock weight a−𝐗a^{-\mathbf{X}}, a rarefaction modulation factor

b⁡(ξ,t):=N⁡(ξ,t)nm,N⁡(ξ,t)=n~R​(ξ+σ​t,t),b(\xi,t):=\frac{N(\xi,t)}{n_{m}},\qquad N(\xi,t)=\tilde{n}^{R}(\xi+\sigma t,t),

and use a modulated relative entropy of the form

∫ℝa−𝐗​b​[Π⁡(n|n~)+12​|q−q~|2]​𝑑ξ.\int_{\mathbb{R}}a^{-\mathbf{X}}b\left[\Pi(n|\tilde{n})+\frac{1}{2}|q-\tilde{q}|^{2}\right]\,d\xi.

The derivatives of bb do not constitute merely an error. After being combined with the rarefaction term already present in the relative entropy identity, they produce the coercive rarefaction dissipation

𝒢R​(t)=1nm​∫ℝa−𝐗​[N​|Qξ|​Π​(n|n~)+|Nt−σ​Nξ|2​|q−q~|2]​𝑑ξ,\mathcal{G}_{R}(t)=\frac{1}{n_{m}}\int_{\mathbb{R}}a^{-\mathbf{X}}\left[N|Q_{\xi}|\Pi(n|\tilde{n})+\frac{|N_{t}-\sigma N_{\xi}|}{2}|q-\tilde{q}|^{2}\right]d\xi,

where Q⁡(ξ,t)=q~R​(ξ+σ​t,t)Q(\xi,t)=\tilde{q}^{R}(\xi+\sigma t,t). This is the mechanism that allows the shock contraction and rarefaction monotonicity to coexist in a single L2L^{2} estimate. At the same time, the shock part controls a characteristic combination of the perturbations rather than the two components separately; preserving this structure is essential for avoiding a loss of the factor λ/δS\lambda/\delta_{S}.

The second difficulty is that the superposition of the rarefaction and the traveling wave is only an approximate solution. The perturbation equations contain source terms

F1=−Nξ​ξ,F2=−∂ξ[(N−nm)(T−qm)+(S−nm)(Q−qm)].F_{1}=-N_{\xi\xi},\qquad F_{2}=-\partial_{\xi}\left[(N-n_{m})(T-q_{m})+(S-n_{m})(Q-q_{m})\right].

The two waves propagate in opposite directions: the rarefaction wave has negative characteristic speed, whereas the traveling wave to the right. Their spatial separation therefore yields exponentially decaying interaction terms. We exploit this separation in both L1L^{1}- and L2L^{2}-based estimates and show that the mixed source terms are integrable in time. These interaction estimates are absent in the traveling wave contraction theory of [3] and in the rarefaction wave analysis of [25].

The third difficulty comes from the degenerate dissipation of (1.1): diffusion acts only on nn, while the qq-equation is hyperbolic. In the basic estimate, the derivative qξ−q~ξq_{\xi}-\tilde{q}_{\xi} is expressed through the parabolic component and its derivatives; the time-derivative term produced by this substitution is treated by integration by parts in time. In the first-order estimate, the same coupling is used to recover ∫0t‖∂ξ(q−q~)‖2​𝑑τ\int_{0}^{t}\|\partial_{\xi}(q-\tilde{q})\|^{2}\,d\tau from the strong dissipation of the nn-equation. This part is inspired by the structural replacement used for strong rarefaction waves in [25], but here it must be compatible with the traveling wave weight, the time-dependent shift and the composite-wave source terms.

These ingredients yield a closed a priori estimate consisting of the H1H^{1} norm of the perturbation, the parabolic dissipation, the shift dissipation, the traveling wave weighted dissipation and the new rarefaction dissipation 𝒢R\mathcal{G}_{R}. A standard continuation argument then gives global existence. Finally, the time integrability of the first and second derivatives implies decay of the perturbation in L∞L^{\infty}, while the shift equation gives 𝐗˙​(t)→0\dot{\mathbf{X}}(t)\to 0 and hence 𝐗⁡(t)/t→0\mathbf{X}(t)/t\to 0.

It is particularly useful to compare our argument with the composite-wave result of Kang, Vasseur and Wang [16] for the one-dimensional barotropic Navier–Stokes equations. They proved the time-asymptotic stability of a composite wave consisting of a 1-rarefaction wave and a 2-viscous shock. Their proof replaces the classical anti-derivative approach for shocks by the aa-contraction with shifts in the BD effective variables

h=u−(ln⁡v)x.h=u-(\ln v)_{x}.

The weight and the shift are attached to the shock component, while the errors caused by the non-exact superposition are controlled by spatial separation of the two waves. In their weighted relative-entropy identity, the rarefaction contribution itself has the favorable sign: the good part contains

∫ℝa​uξR​p​(v|v~)​𝑑ξ,\int_{\mathbb{R}}a\,u^{R}_{\xi}\,p(v|\tilde{v})\,d\xi,

which is nonnegative because a>0a>0, uξR>0u^{R}_{\xi}>0, and the relative pressure p⁡(v|v~)p(v|\tilde{v}) is nonnegative. Hence this term enters the energy identity with a dissipative sign.

This point is substantially different for the chemotaxis system considered here. In the unmodulated weighted relative-entropy identity, the rarefaction derivative does not produce a sign-definite coercive term. In particular, it gives the mixed contribution

𝐁9​(t)=∫ℝa−𝐗​Nξn~​(n−n~)​(q−q~)​𝑑ξ,\mathbf{B}_{9}(t)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}a^{-\mathbf{X}}\frac{N_{\xi}}{\tilde{n}}(n-\tilde{n})(q-\tilde{q})\,d\xi,

whose sign is indefinite. Thus, in contrast with the barotropic Navier–Stokes case, the rarefaction contribution is initially a bad term rather than part of the good dissipation. A main new ingredient of the present paper is to introduce the additional rarefaction modulation

b⁡(ξ,t)=N⁡(ξ,t)nmb(\xi,t)=\frac{N(\xi,t)}{n_{m}}

in the weighted relative entropy. The derivatives btb_{t} and bξb_{\xi} then combine with 𝐁9(b)\mathbf{B}_{9}^{(b)} so that

𝐁9(b)+𝒬b=−𝒢R+∑j=14ℛR,j,\mathbf{B}_{9}^{(b)}+\mathcal{Q}_{b}=-\mathcal{G}_{R}+\sum_{j=1}^{4}\mathcal{R}_{R,j},

where 𝒢R\mathcal{G}_{R} is positive and the four remainders are either absorbable or integrable in time. This rarefaction conversion mechanism is isolated in Lemma 3.5. It is the key point that allows the shock-contraction structure and the rarefaction dynamics to be combined for (1.1).

There is also a structural difference in the recovery of the missing derivative dissipation. The barotropic Navier–Stokes argument uses the BD effective variable to obtain the basic estimate and then returns to the classical variables. Here the hyperbolic component qq has no direct diffusion, and we instead exploit the exact coupling in (1.1) to express the spatial derivative of the qq-perturbation through the parabolic component; the resulting time derivative is handled by integration by parts in time. Thus the present proof follows the same broad aa-contraction-with-shift philosophy, but both the rarefaction coercivity and the recovery of the hyperbolic dissipation require mechanisms specific to the chemotaxis system.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we introduce the relative quantities, construct the smooth approximate 1-rarefaction wave, recall the 2-viscous shock profile, define the weight and the shift, and derive the perturbation system for the shifted composite profile. Section 3 is devoted to the a priori estimates and the proof of Theorem 1.1. The basic estimate combines the weighted relative entropy for the shock with the rarefaction modulation described above; the higher-order estimates then recover the full H1H^{1} dissipation and complete the nonlinear stability argument.

2 Preliminaries

In this section, we collect the relative-entropy quantities used below, construct a smooth approximation of the 1-rarefaction wave, recall the 2-viscous shock profile, and define the time-dependent shift 𝐗⁡(t)\mathbf{X}(t) and the corresponding composite profile.

2.1 Relative quantities

For a smooth scalar or vector-valued function ff, its relative function with respect to two states uu and vv is defined by

f⁡(u|v):=f⁡(u)−f⁡(v)−∇f​(v)⋅(u−v).\displaystyle f(u|v):=f(u)-f(v)-\nabla f(v)\cdot(u-v). (2.1)

For

Π⁡(n):=n​ln⁡n−n,n>0,\Pi(n):=n\ln n-n,\qquad n>0,

we write

Π⁡(n1|n2)=Π⁡(n1)−Π⁡(n2)−Π′​(n2)​(n1−n2).\Pi(n_{1}|n_{2})=\Pi(n_{1})-\Pi(n_{2})-\Pi^{\prime}(n_{2})(n_{1}-n_{2}). (2.2)
Lemma 2.1.

Fix n−>0n_{-}>0. There exist constants δ∗>0\delta_{*}>0 and C>0C>0 such that if

0<δ<δ∗,|n1n2−1|<δ,n−2<n2<2​n−,0<\delta<\delta_{*},\qquad\left|\frac{n_{1}}{n_{2}}-1\right|<\delta,\qquad\frac{n_{-}}{2}<n_{2}<2n_{-},

then

Π⁡(n1|n2)≥n22​[(n1n2−1)2−13​(n1n2−1)3],\Pi(n_{1}|n_{2})\geq\frac{n_{2}}{2}\left[\left(\frac{n_{1}}{n_{2}}-1\right)^{2}-\frac{1}{3}\left(\frac{n_{1}}{n_{2}}-1\right)^{3}\right], (2.3)

and

Π⁡(n1|n2)≤n22​[(n1n2−1)2−13​(n1n2−1)3]+C​δ​|n1n2−1|3.\Pi(n_{1}|n_{2})\leq\frac{n_{2}}{2}\left[\left(\frac{n_{1}}{n_{2}}-1\right)^{2}-\frac{1}{3}\left(\frac{n_{1}}{n_{2}}-1\right)^{3}\right]+C\delta\left|\frac{n_{1}}{n_{2}}-1\right|^{3}. (2.4)
Proof.

Set

w:=n1n2−1.w:=\frac{n_{1}}{n_{2}}-1.

Then

Π⁡(n1|n2)=n2​[(1+w)​ln⁡(1+w)−w].\Pi(n_{1}|n_{2})=n_{2}\big[(1+w)\ln(1+w)-w\big].

For |w|<δ∗<1/2|w|<\delta_{*}<1/2, Taylor’s formula gives

(1+w)​ln⁡(1+w)−w=w22−w36+w412​(1+θ​w)3(1+w)\ln(1+w)-w=\frac{w^{2}}{2}-\frac{w^{3}}{6}+\frac{w^{4}}{12(1+\theta w)^{3}}

2.2 Rarefaction wave

We consider the 1-rarefaction wave connecting the left state (n−,q−)(n_{-},q_{-}) to the intermediate state (nm,qm)(n_{m},q_{m}). In accordance with the definition (1.9), throughout this paper we assume

(nm,qm)∈R1​(n−,q−),(n_{m},q_{m})\in R_{1}(n_{-},q_{-}), (2.5)

so that

h1​(nm,qm)=h1​(n−,q−),λ1​(n−,q−)<λ1​(nm,qm).h_{1}(n_{m},q_{m})=h_{1}(n_{-},q_{-}),\qquad\lambda_{1}(n_{-},q_{-})<\lambda_{1}(n_{m},q_{m}).

Let

λ−:=λ1​(n−,q−),λm:=λ1​(nm,qm).\lambda_{-}:=\lambda_{1}(n_{-},q_{-}),\qquad\lambda_{m}:=\lambda_{1}(n_{m},q_{m}).

Since n>0n>0, both λ−\lambda_{-} and λm\lambda_{m} are negative.

Consider the Riemann problem for the inviscid Burgers equation

{wtr+wr​wxr=0,wr​(x,0)=w0r​(x):={λ−,x<0,λm,x>0.\begin{cases}w^{r}_{t}+w^{r}w^{r}_{x}=0,\\ w^{r}(x,0)=w^{r}_{0}(x):=\begin{cases}\lambda_{-},&x<0,\\ \lambda_{m},&x>0.\end{cases}\end{cases} (2.6)

For t>0t>0, its rarefaction fan is

wr​(x,t)={λ−,x≤λ−​t,x/t,λ−​t≤x≤λm​t,λm,x≥λm​t.w^{r}(x,t)=\begin{cases}\lambda_{-},&x\leq\lambda_{-}t,\\ x/t,&\lambda_{-}t\leq x\leq\lambda_{m}t,\\ \lambda_{m},&x\geq\lambda_{m}t.\end{cases} (2.7)

The 1-rarefaction wave (nr,qr)(n^{r},q^{r}) is defined by

3 Proof of main results

In this section, we investigate the stability of the composite wave for the system (1.1)-(1.2) and prove Theorem 1.1. Applying the standard iteration method, one can readily derive the local well-posedness of the system (2.37). The routine and tedious proof details are omitted for brevity.

Proposition 3.1 (Local existence).

Let n¯\underline{n} and q¯\underline{q} be smooth monotone functions such that

n¯​(x)=n±,q¯​(x)=q±,for±≥1.\underline{n}(x)=n_{\pm},\ \underline{q}(x)=q_{\pm},\ \text{for}\ \pm\geq 1. (3.1)

For any constants M0,M1,κ0,κ¯0,κ1,κ¯1M_{0},M_{1},\kappa_{0},\bar{\kappa}_{0},\kappa_{1},\bar{\kappa}_{1}, with M1>M0>0M_{1}>M_{0}>0 and κ¯1>κ¯0>κ1>0\bar{\kappa}_{1}>\bar{\kappa}_{0}>\kappa_{1}>0, there exists a constant T0>0T_{0}>0 such that if

‖n0−n¯‖H1​(ℝ)+‖q0−q¯‖H1​(ℝ)≤M0,\displaystyle\|n_{0}-\underline{n}\|_{H^{1}(\mathbb{R})}+\|q_{0}-\underline{q}\|_{H^{1}(\mathbb{R})}\leq M_{0},
0<κ0≤n0​(x)≤κ¯0,∀x∈ℝ,\displaystyle 0<\kappa_{0}\leq n_{0}(x)\leq\bar{\kappa}_{0},\quad\forall x\in\mathbb{R},

then system (2.37) has a unique solution (n,q)(n,q) on [0,T0][0,T_{0}] such that

n−n¯∈C⁡([0,T0],H1​(ℝ))∩L2​(0,T0,H2​(ℝ)),\displaystyle n-\underline{n}\in C([0,T_{0}];H^{1}(\mathbb{R}))\cap L^{2}(0,T_{0};H^{2}(\mathbb{R})),
q−q¯∈C⁡([0,T0],H1​(ℝ)),\displaystyle q-\underline{q}\in C([0,T_{0}];H^{1}(\mathbb{R})),

and

sup0≤t≤T0‖(n−n¯,q−q¯)​(⋅,t)‖H1≤M1.\displaystyle\sup_{0\leq t\leq T_{0}}\left\|(n-\underline{n},q-\underline{q})(\cdot,t)\right\|_{H^{1}}\leq M_{1}.

Moreover,

κ1≤n⁡(x,t)≤κ¯1,∀(x,t)∈ℝ×[0,T0].\displaystyle\kappa_{1}\leq n(x,t)\leq\bar{\kappa}_{1},\quad\forall(x,t)\in\mathbb{R}\times[0,T_{0}]. (3.2)

3.1 Relative entropy estimate

In this subsection, we shall estimate the relative entropy function Π⁡(n|n~−𝐗)​|q−q~−𝐗|22\Pi(n|\tilde{n}^{-\mathbf{X}})\frac{\left|q-\tilde{q}^{-\mathbf{X}}\right|^{2}}{2}, which plays a crucial role in deriving the L2L^{2} energy estimate. To this end, we consider employing the classical relative entropy method, which originally introduced by Dafermos[7] and Diperna[9] in the context of establishing the L2L^{2} stability and uniqueness of Lipschitz solutions to the hyperbolic conservation laws endowed with convex entropy.

To apply the relative entropy method, we rewrite (1.1) into the following general system of viscous conservation laws:

∂tU+∂ξ[A⁡(U)]=∂ξ[M⁡(U)​∂ξ∇η​(U)],\partial_{t}U+\partial_{\xi}[A(U)]=\partial_{\xi}[M(U)\partial_{\xi}\nabla\eta(U)], (3.7)

Proof of Proposition 3.2.

The a priori estimate (3.4) follows from Lemmas 3.6 and 3.8. Moreover, in view of (2.39), one can see that

3.2.2 Proof of Theorem 1.1

We now show how Proposition 3.2 implies Theorem 1.1.

nx​x​(t,x)−n~x​xS​(x−σ​t−𝐗⁡(t))∈L2​(0,∞,L2​(ℝ)),n_{xx}(t,x)-\tilde{n}^{S}_{xx}(x-\sigma t-\mathbf{X}(t))\in L^{2}(0,\infty;L^{2}(\mathbb{R})),

+‖ϕξ​ξ‖​‖(n​q−n~​q~)ξ‖+‖ϕξ​ξ‖​‖F1+F2‖.\displaystyle+\|\phi_{\xi\xi}\|\|(nq-\tilde{n}\tilde{q})_{\xi}\|+\|\phi_{\xi\xi}\|\,\|F_{1}+F_{2}\|.

𝐗˙​(t)⟶0.\dot{\mathbf{X}}(t)\longrightarrow 0.

𝐗⁡(t)t=𝐗⁡(0)t+1t​∫0t𝐗˙​(s)​𝑑s.\frac{\mathbf{X}(t)}{t}=\frac{\mathbf{X}(0)}{t}+\frac{1}{t}\int_{0}^{t}\dot{\mathbf{X}}(s)\,ds.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:
